title: The one-nighter route to St. Louis and Art Blakey joining
summary: After a run through the South and Southwest, Blakey arrives in St. Louis and Dizzy corrects his shuffle beat and teaches him to catch breaks.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, when we did get to Tampa, we got this young fellow, and he played Tampa with us. I think we left Tampa and went to Alabama, we played something at Tuskegee Institute, I think. From Alabama, we went to Louisiana, New Orleans. And from there, we went to Houston, Texas. And we played Dallas and Fort Worth. Then we went up to Oklahoma City, Kansas City, and St. Louis.

All these things were one-nighters. When we got to St. Louis, we had a four-week engagement in a club there that a band called Jeter-Pillars had been playing. A lot of good people had come out of that band. One of them was Clark Terry; of course, Clark was in the Navy at that particular time. But this band was sort of a commercial-type band, and wasn't the hard-swinging kind of band that we had. And we went in this club...
In the meantime, Billy had been calling everybody in New York and everywhere else, trying to find a drummer. So

finally, he came to, us when we were in Kansas City, and said, "Well, when we get to St. Louis, I've got this cat coming in that's from Pittsburgh. He's with Fletcher Henderson's band now. His name is Art Blakey." So I'd never met Art before, and some of the guys knew Art. And I think it was at that particular time, one of the trumpet players, I believe, had... Let's see. No, no. I'm getting ahead of my story.

We were in St. Louis, and Art Blakey arrived and then came in, and we had a rehearsal. I never will forget, in the first rehearsal, we rehearsed some tune... By this time, with everyone writing, we had acquired I guess about 17 or 18 arrangements. Because all during the tour, everybody was writing something.

Anyway, as I said before, Dizzy was the straw boss, and he kicked off this first number with Art Blakey, and we started playing and all of a sudden, Art went into kind of a shuffle rhythm. And Dizzy, his way of stopping the band was, he'd always whistle and wave his hands and say, "Stop, stop, stop the band!" And he pointed at Art Blakey and he said, "Look, don't you ever play like that again as long as you live." Well, everybody laughed, you know. So he told him what he wanted. And Dizzy can play very good drums, you know -- he knows everything about the drums.
So from then on, when we would play, Dizzy sat back next

to the drummer all the time. He used to go through a little dance. And as he would go through this dance, in certain places where the band had certain things, he would make a break, and whenever he would break, Art Blakey would catch him with the drums, like a dancer. This is where this drummer's thing called dropping bombs really began to get popular. Art wasn't the first one to do it, but I think it sort of came on with him because he was in this big band. I think the idea came from Kenny Clarke and later with Max Roach.

But anyway, that was the beginning... Once Art caught on to what was happening, then he didn't look back. He just learned what was happening in the band and went on and dominated, you know, the way a good drummer should do.
